title: Linear and Integer Linear Programming
contribution: Expository opening chapter of the joint book: it fixes the book's notation (primal–dual pairs with bracketed duals, one pricing notation c̄(π) shared with column generation, Dantzig-Wolfe and Lagrangian relaxation, point/ray flags) and sets out ILP formulations, extended formulations, the integrality property and LP-based branch-and-bound and branch-and-cut, with one worked tree and fifteen exercises; no result is flagged as new (pp. 1–42).
problem_entry: No gap is claimed: known LP and ILP material is formalized 'under a common notation' for the decomposition chapters, and the primal simplex is the only LP algorithm presented because column generation is the primal simplex with implicit pricing (pp. 2–3, 22).
key_idea: Pricing as the common core of the simplex method, column generation, Dantzig-Wolfe and Lagrangian relaxation (one SP notation, one reused figure), with any dual vector usable to test optimality and bound the optimum; for ILPs, strength and the integrality property belong to the formulation, and extended formulations project back onto the original variables (pp. 11, 16, 18–19, 24–26).
assumptions: LP in inequality, standard (full row rank) and bounded forms; pure ILP x ∈ Z^n_+, MILP only in Note 1.10; rational data, defended by an irrational counterexample; TU and balanced network-flow structure, consecutive-ones and matching only in exercises; no model library; correctness assumptions: an extreme point exists, κ bounds Σ x_j, c⊺x > 0 for the 1/(1−γ) reading of a gap stop, integer b (and c) for the TU results (pp. 4, 6, 14, 19, 21–28, 30, 35–37, 40–42).
proof_devices: Prop 1.1 (an optimal extreme point exists) by contradiction on the optimal face (p. 7)
Prop 1.3 (dual of the dual) by applying the recipe twice (p. 8)
weak duality by multiplying the two constraint systems by π and x; complementary slackness from sums of non-negative products (Props 1.5, 1.7, pp. 9–11)
Farkas' lemma and strong duality proved constructively with Phase I and the optimal simplex basis (Exercises 1.3, 1.8; pp. 9, 39)
Minkowski–Weyl: full proof left to Nemhauser and Wolsey, replaced by three ideas (Theorem 1.1, p. 5)
Prop 1.9 (integrality property iff conv(A ∩ Z^n_+) = A): an extreme point outside the integer hull plus an objective that selects it uniquely (pp. 26–27)
Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.4 via integer inverses of TU bases, and TU of the transpose plus strong duality (p. 27)
Prop 1.10 (node potentials shift by any α) because α cancels in the reduced cost c_ij − π_i + π_j (p. 28)
lower bound z_LP + κ c̄(π) ≤ z⋆_LP at every simplex iteration, generalized to arbitrary π ≥ 0 (Note 1.4, p. 19; Exercise 1.9, p. 40)
reduced-cost fixing from the lower-bound sensitivity line (1.16): c̄_j > UB − LB fixes x_j = 0, valid with a feasible non-optimal dual (p. 30; upper-bound version Exercise 1.14, p. 41)
row differencing for TU of consecutive-ones matrices; blossom separation as an ILP, then polynomially via the cut form (Exercises 1.13, 1.15; pp. 41–42)
counterexample computed as a table: first ten extreme points of an irrational integer hull, slopes converging to √3 (Table 1.3, pp. 36–37)
experiments: n/a as an evaluation (no test set, baseline, hardware, solver version, time limit or seeds): one branch-and-bound tree of 25 LPs from an unnamed application (root 7064, optimum 7111) worked as an exercise and declared unrepresentative of what premature stopping gains; one computed table; evidence only quoted, not re-run (Dantzig 1963 with Shamir's critique; Koch et al. 2022, LP about 180× and MILP about 1000× faster 2001–2020; Bixby's trick question) (pp. 20–21, 31–32, 36, 38).
positioning: Lineage told as a family (Dantzig the father, the OR Fathers of LP algorithms, Land and Doig the mothers of branch-and-bound, Kantorovich's priority as a soap opera); reference policy declared (personal links, not comprehensive, additions invited); history and solver progress via Bixby, Grötschel, Koch et al. 2022; SCIP for Marco and GENCOL for the other three; the co-authors' IPS/MMCC degeneracy line in Good to Know; GCG not named; 'Gauthier et al. (2018)' possibly S044, unverified (pp. 2, 22–23, 28, 35, 37–38).
writing: Joint teaching voice with two epigraphs, twelve titled Notes, jokes inside definitions, a Good to Know layer, a worked Illustration answered step by step and fifteen exercises including history; six of ten propositions proved in the text; hedges where knowledge stops; small slips survive in the text layer (sign of A⊺π in Corollary 1.3's proof, −∞ for an infeasible node, typos) (pp. 1–42; esp. 3–4, 9–10, 18, 21–23, 25, 27, 31–33, 38–39).
limits_future: Sensitivity analysis local and cautious under degeneracy, no solver range for lower-bound changes, perfect formulations usually unknown, pure cutting planes slow, the integrality property does not make x⋆_LP integral (algorithm selection bias), ILP duality and MILP only referenced, references not comprehensive; future only as pointers to chapters 2–7 (pp. 12–13, 16, 18, 23–26, 30, 33, 37, 40).

method_links.note: Joint voice. Step 2 (one notation) is the chapter's stated purpose and its devices: bracketed duals, the shared c̄(π), the reused Fig. 1.5, the point/ray flag for Dantzig-Wolfe, the primal simplex chosen because column generation is the primal simplex. Step 6 in forward form: readers invited to send missing references for a future edition. Step 4 in small: uncertain items printed as uncertain.

Step 5: 'solvers alone will not suffice'; frameworks are needed to tailor the implementation, SCIP for Marco (GCG is not named in the chapter). Steps 1 and 6 get their vocabulary: extended formulations defined against an 'original' model and projected back onto its variables. Also H5: the integrality property is an attribute of the model, and a positive gap does not rule out another formulation of the same problem. Tension 1 in miniature: Dantzig-Wolfe 'works for every ILP' while frameworks exist for tailoring.

Step 6: the one worked tree is declared unrepresentative of premature-stopping gains; the reference notes declare their selection rule (personal links); Shamir's protocol critique of Dantzig's iteration counts and Koch et al. on evaluating solvers 'without bias' are quoted. Also Taste G1: every algorithm output is a certificate, and early stopping 'trades the optimality certificate' but keeps a 1/(1−γ) guarantee when c⊺x > 0.

Folklore claims stay in the authors' own voice without counts of their own (cycling 'is not an issue', 'only takes approximately 3m iterations', nodes 'usually' grow with the integrality gap); the source and its critique are quoted but the sentence is not narrowed. The tree's dependence on 'idiosyncratic coding details' is recognized without a measurement consequence, matching the skill's stated limitation (no seed or permutation protocol).

Enumeration as a teaching device: Table 1.3 lists extreme points of an irrational integer hull to show that it is not a polyhedron and labels the uncertain last row 'potentially' an extreme point; a six-node matching instance and its relaxation are solved by hand in Exercise 1.15.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Bounds and fixing rules stated for any dual vector
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimality can be tested with any x ≥ 0 and π ≥ 0; the bound z_LP + κ c̄(π) ≤ z⋆_LP holds for arbitrary π ≥ 0 (the groundwork for H1, which says to monitor the Lagrangian bound); reduced-cost fixing needs only a feasible dual. The same device appears in ch. 2 (card S060, Note 2.17, p. 20) and ch. 4 (card S084, Prop 4.12, pp. 38–39); all three are chapters of one book.

In Illustration 1.1, sibling order, eager versus lazy creation of child nodes (nodes 5 and 6) and whether a gap is measured against the current LB or the parent's value (0.0050 against 0.0054) change what is reported.

transferable: Write every model as a primal–dual pair, with the dual variable in brackets after each constraint, so that reduced costs, pricing and bounds can be read off directly (pp. 8, 11).

State lower bounds and reduced-cost fixing for an arbitrary feasible dual vector (z⋆ ≥ π⊺b + κ c̄(π); fix x_j = 0 when c̄_j > UB − LB), so that duals from truncated, heuristic or early-stopped solves still bound and fix (pp. 19, 30; Exercises 1.9 and 1.14, pp. 40–41).
With integer objective coefficients, round a node bound up before the pruning test: ⌈7110.5⌉ = 7111 prunes node 29 against UB = 7111 (p. 31).

When you drop integrality because a formulation has the integrality property, check that your LP algorithm returns an extreme point; the property guarantees that an integer optimum exists, not that the solution returned is integer (p. 26; Exercise 1.11, p. 40).
Before concluding that a problem is hard for LP-based methods, try another formulation: a positive integrality gap belongs to the model, not to the problem (p. 26).

Write the pricing step as an LP over convex combinations (min Σ c̄_j y_j with Σ y_j = 1, or a weighted normalization Σ w_j y_j = 1), so that normalized, IPS-type or MMCC-type pricing rules come from one model (pp. 34–35).

Report a stopping tolerance together with the bound it is measured against: in Illustration 1.1 the same incumbent gives 0.0050 or 0.0054 depending on whether the current best bound or the parent node's value is used (p. 32).

Before comparing node counts across codes, ask when each code creates child nodes: eager creation counts nodes pruned at creation (nodes 5 and 6 in Fig. 1.7), lazy creation never makes them (p. 32); the cross-code consequence is an inference.

Present a classical theorem you only use through a reference for the full proof plus the ideas your later chapters rely on (p. 5), and prove Farkas' lemma and strong duality with the algorithm you have just presented (Exercises 1.3 and 1.8, pp. 9, 39).

When you repeat a folklore performance figure, quote its source together with what the source leaves unspecified (phase, start, pivoting rule), as the chapter does with Dantzig and Shamir (pp. 20–21).
coauthors: Jacques Desrosiers, Guy Desaulniers, Jean Bertrand Gauthier
